case_name: Bontos Grosz c. Succession de Trenk
text:
Bontos Grosz c. Succession de Trenk

2019 QCCS 4616

SUPERIOR COURT

(Civil Division)

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF MONTREAL

No:            500-17-092216-160

DATE:      NOVEMBER 1
ST
,
2019

IN THE PRESENCE OF: THE
HONOURABLE GUYLÈNE BEAUGÉ, J.S.C.

ANNA BONTOS GROSZ

v.

ESTATE OF ARPAD TRENK
Represented by its liquidator Arnon Miller

and

ARNON MILLER

and

RUTH MILLER

Défendants

and

RUT A POCAUSKAS

Mise en cause

JUDGMENT

on an Amended Action for Annulment of a Will

and on a Cross-Demand for Damages

1.

PREVIEW

[
1
]

Dr. Arpad Trenk passed away in 2015, at the âge of 101 years old. At
the time of his death, his assets were valued at about $540,000. In 2004, he
had bequeathed ail his assets to the Plaintiff and her husband in equal shares.
However, in 2012, he executed a new will before the notary Mise en cause,
making the Défendants his universal heirs.

[
2
]

Unable to reconcile her disinheritance with her long-lasting friendship
with Dr. Trenk, the Plaintiff is seeking the annulment of his 2012 will. In her
opinion, he was incompétent at the time he executed that last will, and was
under the Défendants’ undue influence (
captation
).
For the latter, the action is abusive and defamatory, since they hâve always
been concerned with Dr. Trenk’s well-being, and hâve always acted in his best
interest. Consequently, they are each asking $30,000 in damages.

[
3
]

The prépondérant evidence supports the Défendants’ position that Dr.
Trenk was of Sound mind at the time he signed his 2012 will, and that they did
not manipulate him into changing his 2004 will. The action will therefore be
dismissed. The cross demand will also fail, there being no evidence of
defamation or of intentional violation of the Defendant’s right to dignity and
réputation.

2.

CONTEXT

2.1

The deceased and his relationship with the parties
until 2011

2.1.1

The deceased

[
4
]

Dr. Arpad Trenk was born in Slovakia on [...], 1913. He had two brothers in Los Angeles, USA, a sister in Czech Republic,
as well as a sister, nephews and nieces in Israël.

[
5
]

Dr. Trenk emigrated from Israël to Canada in the mid-sixties, and
practised as a dentist out of his modest 4
1/2
apartment located in
downtown Montreal that he kept from 1966 to 2011. He had no family in Canada
and never married. Apart for his professional practice, he enjoyed opéra,
skiing, sailing, and playing chess, and travelled a few times to Los Angeles
and Philadelphia.

[
6
]

Dr. Trenk died in Montreal, on January 15, 2015, at the âge of 101
years old.

2.1.2

The Plaintiff

[
7
]

Born
in the Czech Republic, the Plaintiff Anna Bontos Grosz is 75 years old. She emigrated in Canada in 1966, and shortly thereafter met Dr.
Trenk in a Hungarian restaurant where both used to go on a regular basis. She married Andy Grosz.

[
8
]

Although they were not related, Dr. Trenk would always refer publicly
to the Plaintiff as his niece.

[
9
]

From 1966 to 1997, Dr. Trenk developed a close
relationship with the Bontos/Grosz, including their extended family as of 1987.
He was invited to religious célébrations, birthdays, and family dinners. He
especially cared for the Plaintiffs cooking, and enjoyed playing chess or
sailing with her husband. The Plaintiff and her husband lived close by, and
were also patients of Dr. Trenk.

[
10
]

As of 1997, the friendship between the Bontos/Grosz
and Dr. Trenk intensified after Mr. Grosz retired from his florist business at
âge 67. Dr. Trenk was then 84 years old. They would play chess on a regular
basis. Up until September 2011, Dr. Trenk would hâve dinner at the
Bontos/Grosz’ house several times a week, and the three of them would hâve
brunch together every Sunday at the same bakery.

[
11
]

In 2003, the Bontos/Grosz hosted a big célébration
for Dr. Trenk’s 90
th
birthday.

[
12
]

As of 2004, Dr. Trenk’s lifestyle changed as he
grew older and became weaker. He developed hernia problems, and would no longer
ski, sail, ortravel.

[
13
]

On March 22, 2004, at 91 years old, Dr. Trenk had
his first will draw up by notary Ruta Pocauskas, under which he made the
Plaintiff and her husband his universal legatees in equal shares (hereinafter
“the
2004 WILL”).
He also designated them
as his mandataries. He informed them of the foregoing and handed them a copy of
the will. Over the following years, the Plaintiff helped Dr. Trenk with his
banking operations and his tax returns, but never had to use the mandate.

[
14
]

Dr. Trenk used to hide money in his apartment. In
April 2010, there was an épisode when he panicked, erroneously thinking that he
had been robbed. The Plaintiff reassured him that his money was safe at the
bank. The next day, she went to the bank with him, and found out that he had
transferred $150,000 to his nephews in Israël. However, he had no recollection
of the said transfer.

2.1.3

The Défendants

[
15
]

Arnon Miller and Ruth Miller were married in 1964.
They are respectively 90 and 80 years old and hâve two children.

[
16
]

Having lived in Montreal between 1964 and 1975,
they moved permanently to Ottawa that year. Mr. Miller has
had a prolific business career, and the Défendants are well-off. Since 2000,
they hâve been spending their winters—from the end of November until March—in
Mexico where they own a house.

[
17
]

Mr. Miller had known Dr. Trenk since 1958. From
1975 to 2011, Mr. Miller would see Dr. Trenk occasionally when he would hâve
business in Montreal, but rarely Ms. Miller. Dr. Trenk was also the Défendants’
dentist.

[
18
]

At no time prior to July 2012 was Ms. Miller aware
of Dr. Trenk’s financial situation. However, she was under the impression that
he was not wealthy because of the neglected condition of his apartment. She
also thought that he could not hâve had a big clientèle.

2.2

The Post-Summer 2011 Period

[
19
]

In July 2011, Dr. Trenk had a pacemaker installed
and underwent cataract surgery. The Plaintiff was présent at each of Dr.
Trenk’s medical examinations. That same month, he scored 23 out of 30 at a
Mini-Mental Status Exam

(hereinafter
“MMSE”)

taken atthe St. Mary’s Hospital.

[
20
]

On September 18, 2011, Dr. Trenk was admitted at
the St. Mary’s Hospital for a broken hip. He underwent surgery on September 20.
The same day, the Plaintiff’s husband was admitted at the Jewish General
Hospital (hereinafter
“JGH”)
for a
seizure. As of that day, the latter needed constant attention. In December
2011, he broke his hip, and underwent surgery two days later. In addition, he
developed a pneumonia.

[
21
]

On October 3, 2011, Dr. Trenk was discharged from
hospital and admitted to the
Catherine Booth
Réhabilitation Center

(hereinafter
“C. BOOTH”).
During that period, the Plaintiff
shared her time the best she humanly could between her husband at the JGH and
Dr. Trenk at C. Booth. At that point, the relationship had not changed between
them.

[
22
]

The Plaintiff attended meetings with social workers
at C. Booth who assessed that Dr. Trenk could not return safely to his
apartment, and needed to enter a senior’s home. The Plaintiff became
overwhelmed and exhausted with visiting her husband at the JGH and Dr. Trenk
first at St. Mary’s and then at C. Booth. Looking up for help, she came across
Mr. Miller’s téléphoné number in Dr. Trenk’s address book. She knew of him
although having never met him, and remembered that Dr. Trenk had once visited
him in Ottawa.

[
23
]

The Plaintiff contacted the Défendants and asked
them to assist in visiting one or two senior homes for Dr. Trenk, as she had
only two weeks to find a suitable place. They responded favourably, and arrived
in Montreal around October 24, 2011. It was the first encounter between the
Plaintiff and the Défendants.

[
24
]

Upon their arrivai, the Plaintiff explained that
Dr. Trenk would not be returning to his apartment. Without being asked, Mr.
Miller immediately wrote the Plaintiff a chèque of $5,000 for Dr. Trenk’s
moving expenses. The Plaintiff explained that Dr. Trenk had enough money to
cover his expenses, and did not cash the chèque. Later that day, the Plaintiff
and Mr. Miller drove Dr. Trenk to his apartment to pick up hidden money. Again,
without being asked, Mr. Miller wrote a three months’ rent chèque to break Dr.
Trenk’s lease.

[
25
]

The Plaintiff had made three appointments to visit
senior homes on October 31, 2011: the
Salomon
Résidence

(hereinafter the
“SALOMON”),
the
Vista Résidence
(hereinafter the
“VISTA”),
and the
King David Résidence

(hereinafter the
“KING
DAVID”).
The Défendants drove Dr. Trenk, and the Plaintiff went in her
own car. They visited the Salomon and the Vista, and ail agreed that the
latter, which was new and located very close to the Plaintiff’s résidence, was
nice. Since the Plaintiff had to attend to her husband at the JGH, and their
minds had been set on the Vista, she suggested to the Défendants to pay only a
courtesy visit to the King David. The next day, Dr. Trenk told the Plaintiff
that he had chosen the King David. Although it was fine with her, she was
surprised of that decision in light of their discussion the previous day.

[
26
]

On November 1, Mr. Miller brought Dr. Trenk to the
bank, and noticed that he had a lot of savings.

[
27
]

Between November 1 and 20, 2011, several meetings
were held at C. Booth to préparé Dr. Trenk’s application to the King David. At
the November 15 meeting, the Défendants gifted Dr. Trenk with blankets, sheets
and towels; the latter was very pleased. In the following days, the Plaintiff
drove Dr. Trenk to his apartment to make the plan to empty it.

[
28
]

From January to July 2012, the Plaintiff continued
contacting regularly Dr. Trenk over the phone or visiting him. The latter would
also call her to talk about various issues. Meanwhile, like every year, the
Défendants were away at their Mexico résidence. The Plaintiff had no contact
with them, except for one téléphoné call in February, and Dr. Trenk did not
mention them.

[
29
]

The Défendants returned to Montreal in the spring
of 2012. When they would visit Dr. Trenk, they would occasionally buy him
clothes, blankets, lunches, etc. In total, their gifts, that the Plaintiff
characterized as lavish, amounted to about $250.

[
30
]

Around May 2012, Dr. Trenk mentioned to the
Plaintiff that he wished to modify his 2004 Will in order to gift her sister
Valérie, his friend Erika living in Philadelphia, as well as Dr. Sisklac, his
family doctor. That was a one-time conversation over the phone.

[
31
]

In June, Dr. Trenk asked that three paintings that
he had sold to his mover be returned, so he could give the Plaintiff and the
Défendants one painting each.

2.3

The July 2012 Will

[
32
]

On July 9, 2012, Mr. Miller drove Dr. Trenk to Me
Ruta Pocauskas’ office, the same notary who had prepared his 2004 Will. On
their way, Dr. Trenk who had booked the appointment with the notary told Mr.
Miller that he intended to modify his 2004 Will, and to bequeath a gift to his
family doctor as well as to his accountant.

[
33
]

Me Pocauskas was admitted to the Chambre des
notaires du Quebec in 1978, and retired in 2014. She did not testify at the
hearing, but was examined out of court on September 14, 2016. She then declared
that unlike her habit in files involving elderly people, she did not see the
need to request an expert assessment of Dr. Trenk’s capacity since in her
conversation with him she verified and became convinced that he was apt. He told her that he wanted to modify his 2004 Will. When she asked
him why, he replied that he was no longer close to the Plaintiff, and that the
latter and her husband were no longer taking care of him. He added that he had
been hospitalized consecutive to a hip fracture and that he was living in a
senior’s résidence for semi- autonomous persons, specifying, however, that he
was autonomous.

[
34
]

Me Pocauskas did not ask Dr. Trenk if he knew the
value of his assets. About his paintings, he declared that he wished to
bequeath them to certain people, and she suggested that he drew up a list of
wishes for his liquidator. Dr. Trenk attested that his new will faithfully
represented his last wishes.

[
35
]

Dr. Trenk did not tell the Plaintiff about the 2012
Will, nor about the révocation of her mandate.

2.4 The Post-2012 Will
Period

[
36
]

Dr. Trenk was not aware of the seriousness of Mr.
Grosz’ medical condition, as the Plaintiff herself did not realize that her
husband was dying. Mr. Grosz was supposed to be discharged on August 1, but his
condition worsened and he passed away on August 6, 2012. The next day, the
Plaintiff informed Dr. Trenk of the death of her husband. He had no reaction, and refused to attend the funeral. After the
Shiv’ah
mourning,
the Plaintiff paid Dr. Trenk a visit, but he was cold and did not ask about her
husband.

[
37
]

Not understanding Dr. Trenk’s apparent change of
heart, the Plaintiff called Mr. Miller for an explanation. It was the last
contact between her and the Défendants until January 2015.

[
38
]

On August 2, 2013, Dr. Trenk turned 100 years old.
Mr. Miller took the initiative to organize a célébration in a fancy restaurant.
Dr. Trenk drew the list of guests, among which employées of his senior’s home
and of his bank, but did not include the Plaintiff. Nonetheless, she visited
him and gave him a birthday card the following day. He was very pleased.

[
39
]

Between August 2013 and January 2015, the Plaintiff
had scarce contact with Dr. Trenk.

[
40
]

On January 11, 2015, the Plaintiff had a téléphoné
conversation with Dr. Trenk. He had gone to an emergency the same day, but had
returned to his senior’s home. The next day, he was admitted to the St. Mary’s
hospital consecutive to falling in his bathroom.

[
41
]

On January 15, 2015, Dr. Trenk passed away. Mr.
Miller leamed about it at about 11:00 AM, went straight to the bank, and
executed the following two transactions without informing the bank about the
Dr. Trenk’s death:

• A
transfer of $400,000 from Dr. Trenk’s account to his joint account with his
wife;

•

A transfer of $119,000 from Dr. Trenk’s account to his account.

[
42
]

The Plaintiff was told about Dr. Trenk’s death in
the evening. Dr. Trenk was buried the next day. The Défendants paid for the
funeral and the gravestone, but did not organize the traditional
Shiv’ah
mourning. The Défendants are still
paying a yearly fee for maintaining Dr. Trenk’s grave and planting flowers
every spring.

3.

MATTERS IN DISPUTE

[
43
]

The matters in dispute are as follows:

•

Are two alleged statements of Dr. Trenk to the Plaintiff admissible
under Art. 2870 CCQ?

•

Was Dr. Trenk incompetent at the time he signed his 2012 last will?

•

Was Dr. Trenk subject to undue influence on the part of the Défendants
at ail times relevant to the proceedings?

•

Is the Plaintiffs amended action abusive and is she liable for the
amounts claimed by the Défendants in their cross demand?

4.

ANALYSIS

4.1

Objection under Art. 2870 CCQ

[
44
]

The Plaintiff testified about two statements that
the deceased allegedly made to her. The Défendants opposed the evidence on the
basis of the reliability criteria under Art. 2870 CCQ. The Court took the objection
under reserve.

[
45
]

In the Courts opinion, it is not necessary to
décidé the matter. Indeed, whether or not they hâve been made, the two
statements do not add anything to the evidence.

4.2

Was Dr. Trenk incompetent at the time he signed his
2012 last will?

[
46
]

Freedom to bequeath is recognized in Quebec law.
According to that principle, a person displaying the
required capacity may bequeath ail or part of his or her property the way he or
she chooses, subject to certain legislative provisions
[1]
.

[
47
]

An adult is presumed to hâve the required capacity
to fully exercise his or her civil rights. However, to be able to bequeath, a
testator must not only be legally fit, but must also display the willingness to
make a will. The burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities, a testator’s
lack of capacity to duly express a consent belongs to the party alleging it and
seeking the annulment of the will
[2]
.
It is not sufficient to simply raise doubts about the testator’s capacity
[3]
.

[
48
]

Moreover, a testator’s ability to bequeath is
assessed at the time of the signing of the will
[4]
, and incapacity demonstrated at that
précisé moment entails the nullity of the act. Furthermore, the incompétence
described in
Pagé

v.
Henley
(Succession de)
[5]

as “un état habituel d’aliénation ou de faiblesse
d’esprit” demonstrated in a period contemporary to the will créâtes a
presumption of incapacity of the testator at the time of its signature. In that
situation, the burden of proof is reversed and shifts
[6]
, on a
balance of probabilities, to the party claiming that the will was concluded in
an interval when the testator was capable (“a
lucid interval
[7]
”).

[
49
]

In the leading case
Touchette

v.

Touchette
[8]
, the
Court of Appeal had illustrated what form of incapacity would invalidate a
will:

[...] Non seulement l’aliénation mentale, mais aussi la faiblesse
d’esprit sont cause de nullité de testament, si le « de cujus » ne peut avoir
une compréhension adéquate de l’acte posé, ne peut en mesurer la portée et les
conséquences, s’il n’a pas la volonté de l’apprécier, d’y résister ou d’y
consentir; par contre, le testament sera valide si le testateur jouit de ses
facultés intellectuelles au point de pouvoir envisager les divers éléments qui
doivent déterminer une personne à disposer de ses biens d’une manière plutôt que
d’une autre, de comprendre le sens et de mesurer la portée de la disposition
qu’il va faire, et de s’y arrêter volontairement.

[...]

Avant de discuter de la preuve, ajoutons, suivant la jurisprudence
citée plus haut, qu’il n’est pas suffisant qu’un testateur soit capable de
répondre à des questions ordinaires et familières pour qu’on puisse lui
reconnaître la capacité de tester, il lui faut comprendre le sens et la portée
de la disposition qu’il va faire, comme nous venons de le voir plus haut.
(References omitted)

[
50
]

In
Desharnais
v.
Mailloux
[9]
,
Bélanger, J. mentioned that the évaluation of the capacity to sign a will is a
question of fact, and that the Court will base its decision on ail the
circumstances of a testator’s situation:

[15]

L’évaluation de la capacité de tester est
essentiellement une question de fait. Pour en décider, le juge doit se baser
sur toutes les circonstances.

[16]

Ainsi, la prise de médicaments, une mémoire
défaillante, le fait qu’une personne soit très souffrante et somnolente sont
tous des éléments que le Tribunal doit analyser et placer dans le contexte
général de l’affaire.

[17]

Le caractère déraisonnable du legs est également un
élément à prendre en considération. Cependant, le Tribunal doit se garder de
porter un jugement moral sur la question.

[18]

Enfin, toute la preuve testimoniale, que ce soit
des témoins ordinaires ayant ou non un intérêt, des professionnels ayant
gravité autour de la personne décédée, jusqu’aux experts livrant leurs opinions
sur la question, doit être évaluée, puis mise en contexte.
(References omitted)

[
51
]

In the above cited case, the plaintiff claimed that
the testator was incompetent at the time of his will because of certain
unexpected provisions therein. Bélanger, J. decided as follows:

[124]

La preuve démontre que Richard Desharnais était un
homme contrôlant et qui avait une forte estime de lui-même. Il semble bien
qu’il ait fait toute sa vie selon ses propres volontés, sans trop se préoccuper
des conseils des gens qui l’entouraient.

[125]

Le Tribunal comprend aussi fort bien le désarroi
des enfants lorsqu’ils constatent que leur père donne un droit d’habitation à
une personne avec qui il n’a entretenu aucun lien significatif avant de tomber
malade. Il est aisé de comprendre leur déception et leur incompréhension.

[126]

Cependant, malgré le caractère inusité, pour ne pas
dire déraisonnable des actes intervenus en novembre 2004, le Tribunal doit
tenir compte de l’ensemble de la preuve.

[
52
]

The Court of Appeal confirmed that judgment
[10]

even though the first judge had found the will to be
“unusual, not to say unreasonable.”

[
53
]

Moreover, given the complété freedom to bequeath,
Courts must décidé on the legality of a will, and not its morality
[11]
.
The Court’s rôle is not to try to understand why a testator bequeathed in one
way rather than another, nor to Sound the depths of that person’s soûl. It
rather consists in determining if the evidence shows that, at the time of the
will, the testator did not possess the intellectual faculty to understand the
meaning and to measure the scope of the provision he or she was consenting to.

[
54
]

In the présent matter, was Dr. Trenk in a habituai
State of alienation or weakness of mind (“tvn
état habituel d’aliénation ou de faiblesse
d’esprit”)
at the time he signed his 2012 Will? Without hesitating, the
Court concludes in the négative, the Plaintiff having failed to meet her burden
of proof to establish Dr. Trenk’s incapacity.

[
55
]

Plaintiff testified about a few occurrences where
she noted a confusion with Dr. Trenk (forgetting the gift to his nephews, fear
of having been robbed in his apartment), but at the time she was not at ail
alarmed. In fact, she admitted to not having undertaken any action whatsoever
in connection with by these incidents, including never talking to his doctors
about it, and to having been able to maintain several conversations with the
deceased. She also admitted that she had only seen Dr. Trenk on rare occasions
in 2012, and that she had not seen him for many months prior to his death.

[
56
]

The Plaintiff and the Défendants mainly rely on the
conclusions of their respective expert in psychiatry, who both base their
opinion on their
a posteriori
analysis
of Dr. Trenk’s medical file.

[
57
]

Plaintiff builds her case namely around Dr.
Trenks’s scores at three Mini-Mental State Examinations, or MMSE, undertaken
respectively in July 2011 (score of 23/30), on September 27, 2011 (score of
18/29), and on September 29, 2011 (score of 20/30).

[
58
]

The MMSE consists in a short questionnaire with
some tasks to be accomplished by the person whose mental State is being
evaluated. The MMSE is designed to screen people with neurocognitive
impairment. It is also used to monitor a person’s cognitive status and measure
cognitive décliné in a person with neurocognitive impairment. The maximum score
to the MMSE is 30.

[
59
]

Dr. Daniel E. Frank, the Plaintiffs psychiatrie
expert, testified that the average score of the people présent in the courtroom
at trial would be 29 or 30. He declared that a score of 26 or 27 is worrying,
and that a score of 22 or 23 suggests the patient’s cognitive impairment which
would need to be assessed with other criteria. Dr. Frank illustrated that a
person scoring 23 at the MMSE does not know the date or the season, cannot
remember three objects, and cannot follow simple instructions. For a score of
20 to 22, he said that there is no golden rule, but that professionals will do
a detailed analysis of ail factors.

[
60
]

However, in the Court’s opinion, Dr. Frank’s
analysis is incomplète and/or lacks an open mind. Indeed, on the sole basis of
Dr. Trenk’s scores at his three MMSE, the last one taken on September 29, 2011,
more than eight months prior to the 2012 Will, he convinced himself of Dr.
Trenk’s cognitive impairment prior to his admission at the hospital for a hip
fracture. He did not check to what extent other factors might explain these low
scores. But there is more: his rather ambiguous conclusion renders his
expertise undependable.

[
61
]

Dr. Frank’s mandate consisted in conducting:

[...] an examination of the psychiatrie and cognitive status of Mr.
Arpad Trenk and détermine whether he had any psychiatrie condition or disorder.
If and only if such a disorder was présent, comment upon the impact of such
disorder on Mr. Trenk’s capacity to décidé to create a new will and last
testament on July 9,

2012, and upon his mental capacity to do so at that time and his
susceptibility to be subject to undue influence.

[
62
]

The following is his response:

It is the opinion of the undersigned that The Late Arpad Trenk suffered
a neuropsychiatrie disorder in the last years of his life and that this
disorder rendered him impaired in his cognitive abilities. The official
diagnosis of the disorder according the American Psychiatrie Association’s DSM
5 is that of a major neurocognitive disorder of the Alzheimer type.

Due to this psychiatrie disorder with associated mental impairments,
Mr. Trenk’s ability to make reasoned and rational decisions such as to décidé
to create another will, or to participate lucidly in its création would hâve
been significantly impaired. [...].

Mr. Trenk suffered from a delirium or a dementia during his
hospitalization at the St. Mary’s Hospital in September and October of 2011.
These two conditions are often interrelated and both involve significant
impairments in mentation and judgment. Mr. Trenk scored poorly on the Folstein
mini-mental status examination, an objectified measure of cognition. Further,
there was no significant improvement in these scores from September to November
2011, suggesting more of a chronic dementing condition. His mental status in 2015 had deteriorated further and Alzheimer’s
disease was diagnosed. Neurological imaging documented
brain pathology. Considering that the brain slowly deteriorates, it is most
likely that this neurological pathology would hâve been présent in 2012 or
earlier. This leads to the conclusion that impaired mentation progressed
between these two dates but was in existence in July 2012 and earlier. [...]

Due to the absence of complété neuropsychiatrie information at the
relevant times, I cannot conclude that Mr. Trenk was inapt to décidé to create
a new will and testament or to participate competently in creating one.
However, with the information available, I believe that
it is possible
that he was inapt to do so. [...]
[12]
.

(Emphasis in the exhibit)

[
63
]

Dr. Frank’s expertise does not enlighten the Court
as to Dr. Trenk’s psychiatrie condition at the time of the signing of the 2012
Will. The latter’s medical file constituted at the St. Mary’s shows that he
suffered from a delirium in September 2011. However, nothing in the medical
file suggests that Dr. Trenk was in a
habituai

State of alienation or weakness of mind in the fall of 2011, let alone in July
2012. The prépondérant evidence rather establishes that Dr. Trenk’s delirium
consecutive to his hip surgery of September 2011 was punctual and circumstantial.
Indeed, before Dr. Trenk’s hospitalization following his hip fracture, he was
living alone in his apartment and giving no sign of cognitive impairment.
Besides, the Plaintiff was certainly not worried about him. And the same goes
for his post-surgery period. He did not undergo a MMSE after September 29,
2011, and his score improved between his first and his second September MMSE.
In the Court’s opinion, Dr. Frank worked backwards with the hypothesis that Dr.
Trenk was impaired, and tried to find medical evidence to support that
conclusion. Rather, he should hâve kept an open mind as to what could medically
explain Dr. Trenk sudden disorientation of September 2011.

[
64
]

The Défendants’ expert, the psychiatrist Louis
Côté, did not fall in that pitfall. As it should be, he assumed that Dr. Trenk
did not hâve lasting significant cognitive impairment and allowed the medical
evidence to speak for itself. And as a matter of fact, the evidence of Dr.
Trenk’s functioning prior to his admission at the St. Mary’s shows no cognitive
disorder. The evidence is consistent with Dr. Côté’s finding that the change in
Dr. Trenk’s mental status and cognitive functioning was sudden and did not
last:

The change in Mr. Trenk’s mental status
and cognitive functioning was rather sudden, it started about 5 hours after his
surgery for a left hip fracture, with cognitive impairment, with a resuit of
18/29 on the MMSE on September 27,

2011
.

An improvement was reflected two days later, on September 29, 2011, by
a score of 20/30 on the MMSE.

A significant improvement during the two
days leading up to Mr. Trenk’s discharge from the hospital on October 3, 2011,
is reflected by the fact that clinical notes during those two days showed no
signs of delirium, cognitive impairment, behavioural confusion, or
disorganization. It is also reflected by the fact that these notes showed that
Mr. Trenk had recovered his orientation with respect to time, place and
persons. Indeed, the clinical notes described that Mr.

Trenk as fully oriented on October 2 and 3, 2011, that he was aware
that he was being discharged to a convalescent home, and that he was happy.

In the context of: (1) a good level of
mental and cognitive functioning up until the surgery on September 20, 2011, as
illustrated by Dr. Fung’s assessment of Mr.

Trenk’s independent activities of daily living (2) a sudden onset of a
cognitive impairment due to a delirium in the hours following the left hip
surgery (3) a significant improvement of this clinical course over the next two
weeks; and (4) a stable absence of signs of delirium on the last two days of
his hospitalisation, it is my professional opinion that it is: (a) less likely
that Mr. Trenk had been suffering from moderate or mild neurocognitive disorder
(progressive dementia) before September 20, 2011, and (b) highly probable that
he suffered from a brief and réversible post-operative delirium after his
surgery.

In fact, the diagnostic of post-operative delirium was the diagnostic
hypothesis stated by Dr. Fung of the gériatrie assessment unit on September 29,
2011, and the
“Summary sheet”
for the
hospital discharge on October 3, 2011, did not list a diagnosis of dementia or
Alzheimer’s, but listed the diagnosis of delirium as a complication.
[13]

[
65
]

Moreover, the clinical notes at the C. Booth from
October 3 to November 21, 2011, illustrate no lasting irréversible or severe
confusion associated with cognitive impairment. Indeed, on November 3, a
gériatrie doctor found Dr. Trenk competent to choose his nursing home, and on
Nov. 17, a physiotherapist noted that Dr. Trenk was a “strong-headed
98-year-old man who has his routine.”
[14]

In addition, Dr. Trenk was found competent to sign a lease for his senior’s
home with no opposition from Plaintiff.

[
66
]

Furthermore, Dr. Trenk moved at the
King David
on November 20, 2011. He did not
pass another MMSE, and until September 20, 2013, there is no report of
confusion or diminished capacity. It is only in September 2013 that for the
first time a medical note mentions Dr. Trenk’s temporary confusion concomitant
with a bladder infection. So, for the whole period leading to the Will of July
9, 2012, as well as for the following 14 months, there is no evidence of Dr.
Trenk’s impairment, not even mild or temporary.

[
67
]

In light of the foregoing, the Court finds that Dr.
Trenk was without a shadow of a doubt competent at the time he signed his 2012
Will.

4.3

Was Dr. Trenk subject to undue influence on the
part of the Défendants at ail times relevant to the proceedings?

[
68
]

In civil matters, the party seeking to assert a
right has the obligation to satisfy the Court by the administration of
prépondérant evidence
[15]
:
it’s the burden of proof. It means that in order to win, a litigant must prove
that his or her position is more likely than that of the défendant. Probability
is what is certain at 51%, not at 100%. In other words, proof beyond a doubt of
a fact is not required in civil law; a reasonable degree of certainty—more than
50%—is enough. It is the test of the balance of probabilities:

[...] n’est prouvé que ce qui est certain, voire ce qui est probable,
mais jamais ce qui n’est que possible et encore moins ce qui est imaginé [...].
[16]

[
69
]

The allégation of undue influence in the making of
a will is no exception: the burden to prove it belongs to the one who daims
that the testator was unduly influenced
[17]
. Nonetheless, the evidence may be
indirect and circumstantial, and may resuit from presumptions of fact.
“Suspicious circumstances”
[18]

suggesting that the testator was coerced will prompt the Court to use caution.
For example, without being décisive, the tact that the legatee played an active
rôle in the making of a will shall weigh in the balance
[19]
.
Suspicions, hypothèses or mere possibilities are not sufficient for the
discharge of the burden of proof required, namely that which makes the existence
of a fact more likely than its non-existence. A thousand suspicions are not
worth a proof
[20]
.

[
70
]

In the absence of a définition in the
Civil Code of Quebec
,

continuing case law since the Suprême Court
decision in
Stoneham and Tewkesbury

v.
Ouellet
[21]

has found that undue influence (“
captation”
in French) consists of fraudulent
maneuvers intended to cause a person to bequeath in a way rather than in
another. It is to be noted that it is not illégal to gain the favour of a
testator by zeal or affection, even for one’s own interest. However, it is
illicit to take advantage of this proximity to fraudulently seize the will of a
person, and suggest how to bequeath his or her assets. In
Delli Quadri

v.

Antonacci
[22]
,

the Court of Appeal specified the following:

[8] Rappelons d’abord que celui ou celle
qui invoque la captation doit en faire la preuve en démontrant qu’on s’est
emparé de la volonté du testateur et que les gestes posés l’ont, de façon
déterminante, amené à signer un testament qu’il n’aurait pas signé autrement.
Ces gestes doivent s’apparenter à de la fraude.

Des manifestations de dévouement — sincère ou simulé — de nature à
susciter l’affection ne sont pas suffisantes.
(References omitted)

[
71
]

Undue influence is sometimes obvious. It may also
resuit from a sériés of behaviours that are not conclusive, but which,
combined, constitute fraud. For example, the facts for an heir to call the
notary or to be présent at the signing of the will
[23]
are
to be analyzed with caution. The behaviour that case law associâtes with undue
influence varies from case to case. However, courts generally consider the âge
and health of the testator to appreciate his or her ability to withstand
fraudulent tactics. Often, undue influence is suggested from a proof
established by presumption of facts, because the ill- intentioned heir does not
act openly. Consequently, courts will assess whether the evidence shows
predominantly serious, précisé and concordant presumptions
[24]

making the undue influence theory probable. If so, and if the maneuvers
actually provoked the testator’s decision, the Court will annul the will.

[
72
]

In the recent matter of
Ginsberg

v.

Ginsberg
[25]
,

Vaillancourt, J. made an exhaustive review of
the case law on the concept of undue influence and noted the applicable
principles:

[279]

A person is free to make gifts to whomever he or
she wishes and is also free to designate whomever he or she wishes as the
beneficiary of a life insurance policy or a RIFF.

[280]

The person may therefore exercise that right as he
or she sees fit and make choices that may surprise or disappoint his or her
circle. In exercising that right, he or she may even act unfairly.

[281]

The person must, however, give his or her free and
informed consent when exercising that right.

[282]

Such a decision may be set aside if the person who
invokes undue influence shows “qu’on s'est emparé de la volonté du testateur et
que les gestes posés l’ont, de façon déterminante, amené à signer un testament
qu’il n’aurait pas signé autrement. Ces gestes doivent s’apparenter à de la
fraude. Des manifestations de dévouement — sincères ou simulées — de nature à
susciter l’affection ne sont pas suffisantes.”
(References omitted.)

[
73
]

Proving the manipulation in order to do justice to
the last wishes of a deceased person is not an easy task because crafty people
will be prudent and will act secretly
[26]
.
There will rarely be direct evidence of undue influence, but much more than an
unexpected change in testamentary provisions is required to conclude that
fraudulent tactics were présent
[27]
.

[
74
]

In the matter of
Delli
Quadri
c.
Antonacci
[28]
,
the Court of Appeal found that the fact that the deceased had bequeathed part
of his assets to the people who took care of him at the end of his life was not
“incongruous”:

[33] Finalement, il y a lieu de souligner que le legs aux intimés,
quoique généreux, n’est pas incongru. M. Totaro, qui n’avait pas d’enfant, a
choisi de léguer une partie de ses biens à ceux qui ont pris soin de lui à la
fin de sa vie. Ce faisant, il a nécessairement privé sa petite nièce,
l’appelante, de certains biens, mais il était libre de le faire. Il n’avait pas
d’obligation à son égard et, dans les circonstances révélées par la preuve, le
fait qu’il ait choisi de léguer son immeuble aux intimés s’explique et ne
soulève pas de questions sérieuses quant à l’intégrité de son consentement au
moment où il a modifié son testament en ce sens.

[
75
]

Dr. Frank identified three set of factors
indicating warning signs that undue influence is présent, including:

1.

Social or environmental risk factors such as dependency, isolation, family
conflict and recent bereavement;

2.

Psychological and physical risk factors such as physical disability,
deathbed wills, sexual bargaining, personality disorders, substance abuse and
mental disorders including dementia, delirium, mood and paranoid disorders;

3.

Legal risk factors such as unnatural provisions in a will, or
provisions not in keeping with previous wishes of the person making the will,
and the instigation or procurement of a will by a beneficiary.

[
76
]

In applying that analysis grid, Dr. Frank believes
that Dr. Trenk was subject to undue influence, and that captation did operate:

Ail three of these factors were operative in the présent case.

First, Mr. Trenk was a very old man with medical impairments and social
isolation in that the only individual présent in his life until the Miller
couple arrived in Montreal was Ms. Grosz. A well, a very significant conflict
between the Millers and Ms. Grosz emerged, with pressure on Mr. Trenk to choose
sides. In his medically and psychiatrically impaired State and in context of
his lack of a family or any other close persons in Montreal aside from Ms.
Grosz, he was rendered increasingly dépendent on those around him, either Ms.
Grosz or the Millers.

This social and environmental factor seems to be fulfilled.

Second, there existed clear physical and mental impairments in Mr.
Trenk including delirium and/or dementia as well as significant paranoid traits
and behaviours. This the second “red flag” suggesting undue influence is
fulfilled.

Third, Mr. Trenk altered his previous will in which he had left his
estate to the Grosz couple for understandable reasons, considering his
closeness to them and lack of close family members or other individuals in his
life. He was a friend of some intensity with the Millers but they lived in
another city, and sometimes in another country, and they did not seem to see
each other very often. The involvement of the Millers in Dr. Trenk’s financial
and legal
affairs does
not hâve an
immédiate and apparent justification. Finally, considering the above phrase:
“procurement of a will by a beneficiary,” Mr. Miller himself acknowledged that
he was présent in the notary’s office when Mr. Trenk signed his last will on
July 9,

2012
.

[...] I believe that Mr. Trenk was definitely susceptible to undue
influence on July 9, 2012. Further, in considering the interaction between his
underlying cognitive vulnerabilities and the social factors impinging upon him,
I conclude that
it is probable and most likelv
.
that a State of undue influence occurred on July 9,

2012.
[29]

(Emphasis in the exhibit.)

[
77
]

On the contrary, Dr. Côté is of the opinion that
Dr. Trenk showed no sign of a diminished capacity to create a new will or to
resist undue influence.

[
78
]

As to the presence of undue influence, the Court
disagrees with Dr. Frank’s analysis of the evidence:

•

Regarding what Dr. Frank describes as “social or
environmental risk factors”, the evidence shows that Dr. Trenk was not isolated
at the time of his 2012 Will. For one, the Plaintiff was still in his life and
the Défendants had done nothing to isolate Dr. Trenk or to keep him away from
her. Indeed, she would see him less than prior to her husband’s sickness, but
the Défendants had nothing to do with it. These were the hazards of life.
Moreover, Dr. Trenk was not isolated at his senior’s home, and the Plaintiff
could visit him with no restriction. In addition, Dr. Trenk interacted so much
with the personnel that he invited them to his 100
th
birthday
célébration, a party for which he submitted the list of guests. Furthermore, contrary
to what Dr. Frank testified to, the evidence does not establish at ail that “a
very significant conflict between the Millers and Ms. Grosz emerged, with
pressure on Mr. Trenk to choose sides.” The Court wonders where the Plaintiff’s
expert draws that conclusion from.

•

Concerning the “psychological and physical risk
factors”, the Court already found that Dr. Trenk was clearly competent to
consent to a new will on July 9, 2012.

•

As to “legal risk factors”, Mr. Miller always acted
in the open, and did not try to hide the fact that he occasionally accompanied
Dr. Trenk to the bank, nor that he was présent at the notary’s office on July
9, 2012, at Dr. Trenk’s request. In the preceding winter, the Défendants did
not change their habit to spend several months in Mexico and did not try to
grow doser to Dr. Trenk. They left as usual in early winter and only came back
in the spring. By then, the Plaintiff was already seeing less of Dr. Trenk on
account of her presence at the bedside of her very sick husband. Dr. Trenk
changed his will in favour of the Défendants, and he was free to do so. In
Ruffo
v.
Gohier
(Succession de)
[30]
,
Paquette J.
recalls that the bottom line is that the choice of the heirs belongs to the
testator:

[28]

En effet, le testateur n’a pas de comptes à rendre sur ses choix
testamentaires. Il est libre d’exercer sa liberté de tester comme il l’entend.
Il peut prendre des décisions sévères, même injustifiées envers les
successibles, sans qu’il n’y ait pour autant captation.

[29]

Le testateur peut faire les choix qui, quoique justes à ses yeux,
paraissent injustes à certains. Il peut même choisir d’être injuste ou de
décider autrement qu’en se fondant sur la raison.

[30]

Justes ou non, raisonnables ou non, les choix du
testateur doivent prévaloir, pourvu qu’ils soient les siens.

[
79
]

In light of the above, the Court concludes that the
Plaintiff did not establish that Dr. Trenk was subject to undue influence on
the part of the Défendants when he modified his will on July 9, 2012.

4.4

The Defendant’s Cross Demand: is the Plaintiff’s
Amended Action abusive and is she liable for the damages claimed by the
Défendants?

[
80
]

Arguing that the Plaintiff’s action has no legal
basis and constitutes an abuse of procedure, the Défendants filed a cross
demand and claimed damages of $30,000 each. They submitted that Plaintiff only
raised the alleged incapacity of Dr. Trenk when she initially filed her action
in 2016, long after she had learned that she was no longer a beneficiary under
his will.

[
81
]

The Défendants pleaded that there was no reasonable
basis for the Plaintiff to actually believe that Dr. Trenk did not know what he
was doing when he changed his will in July 2012, and added that her own expert
was only able to attest that it is possible that that the latter had been
unfit. They consider Plaintiff’s action reckless and defamatory.

[
82
]

The Défendants are invoking this Courts decision in

Chiavarolli
v.
Cotellese
[31]
,
where the
plaintiff was found to hâve lied to advance her position to set aside her
father- in-law will:

[51] Plaintiff was unreasonable. She was rash and careless as to the
conséquences of her actions on her sister-in-law. She instituted and pursued an
action without any reasonable expectation that it might succeed. She invoked
facts that she knew did not represent the truth. Such behaviour constitutes
evidence of bad faith and legal impropriety. If anything is évident of bad
faith, it certainly must be where a party knowingly relies on or invokes facts
which she knows are untrue, which she cannot prove, and, adopts a stance in
contrary legal proceeding that most benefit her current personal or family
interests.

[
83
]

Courts hâve the power to sanction abuses of the
procedure
[32]
.
However, a mistaken belief or the weakness of the evidence are not sufficient
to constitute an abuse of the right to sue. As this Court put it in the matter
of
Montebello Real Estate Brokers Associates
Inc.
[33]
,
the
unsuccessful exercise of a right is not in itself wrong:

[82] (...) L’exercice infructueux d'un droit revendiqué devant un
tribunal n’est pas en soi fautif. « J’ajoute que, même en matière d’abus du
droit d’ester en justice, il faut éviter de conclure à l’abus dès que la thèse
mise de l’avant est quelque peu fragile sans être abusive. Même dans les
provinces de
common law
qui
reconnaissent la notion de “dépens avocat client”, le peu de fondement d’une
demande ne suffit pas à lui seul pour justifier l’octroi de tels dommages.
(Young
c.
Young,

1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1993] 4 R.C.S. 3, 134) ». Le tribunal n’est pas convaincu que cette demande en
justice soit abusive parce qu’elle ne serait supportée par aucune preuve
susceptible de justifier les conclusions recherchées. Le rejet d’un recours ne
signifie pas pour autant qu’il ait été exercé de manière déraisonnable ou de
mauvaise foi.

[
84
]

In the matter of
Royal
LePage commercial Inc.
[34]
,
the Court of
Appeal found that to conclude that a litigant abused of the right to sue, the
evidence must show bad faith, such as the intention to inconvenience the
opponent rather than the desire to advance one’s own rights, as well as signs
of recklessness:

[45]

Pour conclure en l’abus, il faut donc des indices de mauvaise foi
(telle l’intention de causer des désagréments à son adversaire plutôt que le
désir de faire reconnaître le bien-fondé de ses prétentions) ou à tout le moins
des indices de témérité.

[46]

Que faut-il entendre par témérité? Selon moi, c’est le fait de mettre
de l’avant un recours ou une procédure alors qu’une personne raisonnable et
prudente, placée dans les circonstances connues par la partie au moment où elle
dépose la procédure ou l’argumente, conclurait à l’inexistence d’un fondement
pour cette procédure. Il s’agit d’une norme objective, qui requiert non pas des
indices de l’intention de nuire, mais plutôt une évaluation des circonstances
afin de déterminer s’il y a lieu de conclure au caractère infondé de cette
procédure.

Est infondée une procédure n’offrant aucune véritable chance de succès,
et par le fait, devient révélatrice d’une légèreté blâmable de son auteur.
Comme le soulignent les auteurs Baudouin et Deslauriers, précités : « L’absence
de cette cause raisonnable et probable fait présumer sinon l’intention de nuire
ou la mauvaise foi, du moins la négligence ou la témérité ».
(References omitted).

[
85
]

In the case at hand, the Plaintiff is unsuccessful
in her claim because she failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities,
Dr. Trenk’s lack of capacity to duly express a consent.

[
86
]

The Plaintiffs had doubts caused by the
astonishment of being suddenly disinherited, after having been told of the
content of the Will of 2004. The unexpected bequeath to the Défendants could
not leave her indifferent
[35]
.

[
87
]

But, there is no evidence to support the position
of the Défendants that the Plaintiff was only out to harm them. Some of her
allégations may be harsh (it is unfortunate that the adversarial judicial
System often encourages some litigants or their attorneys into drafting
clumsily ignited allégations to convince the Court). However, at trial, the
Plaintiff adopted a sober behaviour and although she had an erroneousperception
of Dr. Trenk’s mental State, she did not lie, unlike in the
Chiavaralli
case. The Court considers that
she has not been reckless.

[
88
]

Moreover, the Défendants did not elaborate on their
alleged damages. In fact, their testimonies show that they are especially
taking offence in Plaintiffs position regarding Dr. Trenk’s mental State at the
time of the 2012 Will, a position that they consider “insulting, deeply
offensive to anyone who knew (him), and an affront to his memory.” To be upset,
angry or sad that the Plaintiff has dared to doubt Dr. Trenk’s capacity does
not constitute ground for action. Consequently, the cross demand will fail.

[
89
]

Finally, the Plaintiff will bear the legal costs.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
90
]

DISMISSES
Plaintiffs amended action;

[
91
]

MAINTAINS
the defence of the défendants;

[
92
]

DISMISSES
the cross demand of the Défendants;

[
93
]

WITH LEGAL COSTS
in favour of the Défendants, includina their expert fees in the amount
of $18,250
